text:
We have more planning engineers than ever. Every contract comes with a planning specification, DCMA checks, a WBS standard and a monthly report template. So why are our projects still late?

The latest numbers are hard to ignore:
• 79 % of Middle East project organisations had delays in the past year, and 81 % had cost overruns (PwC Middle East Capital Projects & Infrastructure Survey, 2025).
• On 2,410 projects in 122 countries that ended in claims or disputes, the time extensions claimed average 66 % of the planned schedule. Even on projects due since 2020, it is 49 % (HKA CRUX, 2026).
• In the Middle East that figure was 81 %, the highest of any region (HKA CRUX, 2024).
• Design failures were behind the claims on 40 % of those projects, and scope change on 33 % (HKA CRUX, 2026).
• 38 % of the PwC respondents put their delays down to regulatory requirements.

Look at the causes these reports name: design failures, scope changes, approvals. Studies of UAE projects add late drawing approvals, slow owner decisions and unrealistic contract durations. Not one of them is a scheduling software problem.

My view, after 18 years in project controls:

1. We measure the schedule, not the forecast. A specification checks whether the schedule is built correctly: logic, codes, float, activity count. Nobody checks whether last quarter's forecast came true.
2. The plan is owned by planning, not by the people who decide. Delays come from approvals, changes and decisions, and those rarely sit in the schedule with a duration and an owner.
3. The date comes first and the plan is built backwards to meet it. Then we call the gap "recovery".
4. Change is analysed months later, as a claim. By then the planner is writing history, not planning.

What would change it: put every decision in the plan with an owner and a due date, report overdue decisions in every meeting, assess the time impact of a change in the week it happens, and track forecast accuracy as a KPI of the planning team.

More planners will not fix a decision problem. Better decisions, made on time, will.

Planners and project managers: what do you think is the real reason?
